questions.prompt: A technician plates 0.1 mL of a 1/1,000,000 dilution of phage stock on a bacterial lawn and counts 50 plaques. About how many phages per mL were in the original stock?

options.text: 5 × 10^7 (50 million)
5 × 10^6 (5 million)
5 × 10^5 (500 thousand)

questions.explanation: Each plaque = one original phage. 50 plaques ÷ 0.1 mL = 500 per mL of the dilution; × 1,000,000 = 5 × 10^8 per mL.

questions.prompt: One phage infects a bacterium and about 300 phages burst out. If each of those infects a new cell and each cell releases about 300, how many phages are there after the second round?

options.text: About 90,000
About 900
About 3,000
About 600

questions.explanation: 300 × 300 = 90,000 — why phage therapy is described as self-amplifying.

questions.prompt: A patient with an E. coli infection is mistakenly given a phage that infects only Streptococcus pyogenes. What happens?

options.text: The phage infects E. coli anyway, since any phage can infect any bacterium once it is inside the body
The phage enters the lysogenic cycle in the patient's cells and waits until S. pyogenes shows up
The phage switches to infecting the patient's own gut-lining cells, since it can't find its usual host
The phage finds no host cells it can infect, can't reproduce, and eventually degrades — and the E. coli infection continues

questions.explanation: Phages are highly specific. Without matching host cells they can't multiply and simply break down (self-eliminating).

questions.prompt: A throat culture grows Streptococcus pyogenes, but no scarlet fever toxin is detected. Which explanation fits the lecture?

options.text: Scarlet fever toxin is made only by Clostridium botulinum
This strain doesn't carry the prophage that has the scarlet fever toxin gene
The patient's antibodies erased the toxin gene from the bacterial chromosome
The bacteria are in the lytic cycle, which stops all toxin production

questions.explanation: The toxin gene is on prophage DNA, not in the bacterial genome. Only lysogenized strains can make it.

questions.prompt: A lysogenized culture is kept in ideal, stress-free conditions for months. What happens to the prophage?

options.text: It bursts all the cells within a day or two, since a prophage always switches to the lytic cycle quickly
It is cut out and digested by the host, since the host recognizes the prophage as foreign DNA
It stays integrated and is copied into every new cell; no phages are made, since there is no stress to trigger induction
It turns into a plasmid and is passed to neighboring cells, so the original cells lose it over time

questions.explanation: Induction occurs when host cells become stressed. Without stress, the prophage rides along through every division.

questions.prompt: Which pair of course viruses differ in ALL three features: nucleic acid type, capsid shape, and envelope?

options.text: HPV and SARS-CoV-2
Influenza and tobacco mosaic virus
SARS-CoV-2 and influenza
Ebola virus and tobacco mosaic virus

questions.explanation: HPV: DNA, polyhedral, naked. SARS-CoV-2: RNA, helical, enveloped. SARS-CoV-2/influenza are both RNA, helical, enveloped; Ebola and TMV are both helical.

questions.prompt: Why does the amount of phage in phage therapy rise and fall with the infection?

options.text: The patient's own cells make more phages when the infection is worse, and stop when the fever breaks
Phages multiply only inside the target bacteria, so their numbers rise with the infection and fall once no hosts are left
The doctor adds more phages each day based on the patient's symptoms, the same way antibiotic doses are adjusted
Phages sense how many bacteria are present and release a chemical signal that tells them how fast to divide

questions.explanation: Small dose, self-amplifying, self-eliminating: a phage is a non-living obligate intracellular parasite.

questions.prompt: Which item from the instructor's 'properties of viruses' checklist is something viruses SHARE with living organisms?

options.text: They have their own machinery for synthesizing proteins
They can mutate and acquire adaptations
They replicate themselves without a host
They process energy

questions.explanation: The checklist says viruses lack metabolic enzymes and protein-synthesis machinery, don't process energy, and can't replicate themselves — but they can mutate and adapt.

questions.prompt: If a C. botulinum culture were 'cured' of its prophage, what would change?

options.text: It could no longer make botulism toxin, since that gene is on the prophage
It would immediately burst, since every lysogenized cell needs its prophage to survive
Nothing — the toxin gene is in the bacterial chromosome
It would make more botulism toxin, since the phage no longer competes for resources

questions.explanation: Botulism toxin is encoded on prophage DNA, not the bacterial genome.

questions.prompt: A phage's DNA is destroyed right after it is injected, but the empty capsid stays attached outside. What happens?

options.text: The bacterium uses the capsid as a template to copy the phage
The empty capsid enters the cell and builds new phages
No new phages are made, since the genome carries all the instructions
The cell bursts anyway, releasing about 300 empty capsids

questions.explanation: Only the genome enters; it directs biosynthesis. Without it, the host has no instructions to build phages.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the history of virology is FALSE?

options.text: The word 'virus' wasn't used until the 1930s.
Wendell Stanley saw the first virus with an electron microscope in 1892.
Félix d'Hérelle discovered bacteriophage around 1916.
The first virus seen with the electron microscope was tobacco mosaic virus.
Ivanovsky discovered the 'filterable infectious poison' around 1892.

questions.explanation: False — Stanley saw viruses in 1935; electron microscopes were invented in the 1930s.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the lytic cycle is FALSE?

options.text: During release, the host cell lyses and new virions burst out.
Lysozyme helps the phage genome get through the peptidoglycan cell wall.
During biosynthesis, the phage uses its own ribosomes to make capsid proteins.
The phage stores energy in its structure when assembled, like a jack-in-the-box.
During maturation, viral components are assembled into new virions.

questions.explanation: False — viruses have no ribosomes; the host cell's machinery makes the phage parts.

questions.prompt: Which statement about plaque assays is FALSE?

options.text: Each plaque is a colony of phages growing on top of the agar.
Serial dilution lets you back-calculate the phage concentration.
Each plaque represents one phage in the original sample.
The bacteria are plated thickly enough to form a lawn.
A plaque is a clear zone where phages killed bacteria and spread to neighbors.

questions.explanation: False — a plaque is a zone of dead bacteria (a 'ring of death'), not a colony.

questions.prompt: Explain why viruses are called non-living obligate intracellular parasites. Use the lytic cycle to show what a phage brings to the infection and what the host cell must supply.
questions.explanation: Viruses don't meet the criteria for life: they lack enzymes for metabolism and machinery for making proteins, don't process energy, and can't reproduce on their own. They are obligated to get inside a cell to be reproduced, and the cell is harmed or killed in the process (parasite). In the lytic cycle the phage brings only a few things: attachment proteins/tail fibers to bind the host, lysozyme, and its genome (DNA) — the instructions — which is injected using energy stored when the phage was assembled. The host supplies everything else: it copies the phage genome and transcribes and translates its genes (biosynthesis), and the parts are assembled into new virions (maturation) until the cell lyses and releases them.

questions.prompt: A patient has a resistant bacterial gut infection. Compare treating it with a broad antibiotic, with phage therapy, and with a fecal transplant, giving one advantage and one drawback of each.
questions.explanation: Broad antibiotic (e.g., Cipro): advantage — works without knowing the exact microbe; drawbacks — non-specific, killing good bacteria (setting up other infections like yeast infections), needs large doses for 10–14 days, and resistance is growing. Phage therapy: advantages — highly specific (only the target bacteria), small self-amplifying dose, self-eliminating; drawback — you must identify the exact bacterium to match a phage, which adds tests and cost. Fecal transplant (from a healthy donor, like d'Hérelle's filtrate idea without filtering): advantage — delivers a mix of good phages and microbes without isolating a specific phage, and it is working against C. difficile; drawback — it is non-specific and less controlled.
